hints: Focus on what hot alcoholic NaOH does to a bromoalkane, and why X must be able to form two different alkenes.
Identify which starting structure can eliminate HBr in two different directions to give one ring double bond and one exocyclic double bond.
Think about adding Br2 to each alkene and counting chiral centres, one dibromide needs two chiral centres for four optical isomers while the other needs a plane of symmetry.
walkthrough:
**Recognise the elimination reaction**

Great start, hot alcoholic NaOH means dehydrohalogenation. X loses HBr to form alkenes with formula $\text{C}_7\text{H}_{12}$.

$$\text{C}_7\text{H}_{13}\text{Br} + \text{NaOH (alc, hot)} \rightarrow \text{C}_7\text{H}_{12} + \text{NaBr} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Work out what Y and Z must be**

To get two alkenes, X must have two different sets of neighbouring H atoms to remove. One alkene, Y, on adding $\text{Br}_2$ gives a dibromide with four optical isomers.

$$\text{Y (C}_7\text{H}_{12}) + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_7\text{H}_{12}\text{Br}_2$$

**Interpret the four optical isomers clue**

Four optical isomers means two chiral centres. That is $2^2 = 4$ stereoisomers, two pairs of enantiomers. This fits addition to 1-methylcyclohex-1-ene to give 1,2-dibromo-1-methylcyclohexane, where both C1 and C2 are chiral.

**Interpret the non-chiral clue**

The other alkene, Z, on adding $\text{Br}_2$ gives an achiral dibromide. This fits methylenecyclohexane, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}\text{=CH}_2$. Addition gives $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}\text{(Br)(CH}_2\text{Br)}$, where C1 is attached to two identical ring $\text{CH}_2$ groups, so it has a plane of symmetry and is non-chiral.

**Link back to X**

Only 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane can eliminate in two ways to give exactly those two alkenes. Loss of a ring H gives 1-methylcyclohexene, loss of a methyl H gives methylenecyclohexane. So X must be option A.

options.A: 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane is tertiary and has H atoms on the ring and on the methyl group. Elimination gives Y = 1-methylcyclohex-1-ene and Z = methylenecyclohexane. Bromination of Y gives 1,2-dibromo-1-methylcyclohexane with two chiral centres, hence four optical isomers. Bromination of Z gives 1-bromo-1-bromomethylcyclohexane which is symmetrical and achiral. Both conditions are met.
options.B: Bromomethylcyclohexane is a primary bromide. Elimination of HBr can only use ring H atoms to give essentially one alkene, methylenecyclohexane. It cannot produce two different alkenes Y and Z, so it fails the first observation.
options.C: 2-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane could give two alkenes, 1-methylcyclohex-1-ene and 3-methylcyclohex-1-ene. However bromination of 3-methylcyclohex-1-ene gives 1,2-dibromo-3-methylcyclohexane which still has chiral centres and is chiral, not non-chiral. So it cannot give the required achiral product.
options.D: The 1-methyl-3-bromo (or 1-methyl-4-bromo) isomer eliminates to give alkenes where the double bond is in the ring with the methyl substituent still on a separate carbon. Bromination of both of these alkenes gives dibromides that retain chiral centres. Neither dibromide is the highly symmetrical achiral type formed from an exocyclic alkene, so D does not fit.
